pericopes.text: Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but such as is good for building up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear. Don’t grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.

echoes.text: But they rebelled, and grieved his holy Spirit: therefore he was turned to be their enemy, and he himself fought against them.
echoes.note: 'Don't grieve the Holy Spirit of God' alludes to Israel who 'rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit.' Volume is high (the rare collocation 'grieve' + 'Holy Spirit' is virtually unique to Isa 63:10 in the OT) and coherence is excellent. One of the strongest non-quotation allusions in the chapter.

echoes.text: A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but deceit in it crushes the spirit.
echoes.note: 'Let no corrupt speech... but such as is good for building up... that it may give grace' echoes wisdom's 'a gentle tongue is a tree of life' (cf. 10:31-32, 12:18). Volume is low and the tongue-ethics field is diffuse, so the echo is faint though coherent with the speech-edification theme.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to him, Go through the midst of the city, through the midst of Jerusalem, and set a mark on the foreheads of the men that sigh and that cry over all the abominations that are done in its midst.
echoes.note: 'In whom you were sealed for the day of redemption' may echo the protective mark/seal set on the faithful before judgment. Volume is low and the link debated, but the eschatological sealing-for-deliverance motif coheres.

pericopes.text: Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander, be put away from you, with all malice. And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.

echoes.text: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth, keeping loving kindness for thousands, forgiving iniquity and disobedience and sin; and that will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, and on the children’s children, on the third and on the fourth generation.”
echoes.note: 'Be kind... tenderhearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you' grounds the imitation of God in the merciful self-revelation 'merciful and gracious... forgiving iniquity.' Volume is moderate and coherence high: divine forgiving compassion is the model for human forgiveness (imitatio Dei). Availability is a cornerstone OT text.

echoes.text: Yahweh is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness. He will not always accuse; neither will he stay angry forever. He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us for our iniquities. For as the heavens are high above the earth, so great is his loving kindness toward those who fear him. As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us. Like a father has compassion on his […]
echoes.note: 'As a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion' and 'merciful and gracious, slow to anger' parallel 'be kind to one another, tenderhearted' as the gracious God's image. Volume is moderate; the psalm liturgically extends Exod 34:6-7, reinforcing recurrence of the compassion source.

echoes.text: Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all wrongs.
echoes.note: Putting away 'all bitterness, wrath, anger... and malice' in favor of forbearing love echoes 'hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all offenses.' Volume is low and the parallel is thematic, so the echo is faint though coherent with the forgiveness ethic.

pericopes.text: Be therefore imitators of God, as beloved children. Walk in love, even as Christ also loved you, and gave himself up for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling fragrance.

echoes.text: “Speak to all the congregation of the children of Israel, and tell them, ‘You shall be holy; for I, Yahweh your God, am holy.
echoes.note: The call to 'be imitators of God' reworks the imitatio Dei formula 'You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy,' the foundational ground of Israelite ethics. Volume is moderate (conceptual not verbal), but coherence is high since the surrounding paraenesis on sexual purity and conduct 'as becomes saints' tracks Leviticus 19's holiness code.

echoes.text: You shall be perfect with Yahweh your God.
echoes.note: 'You shall be blameless before the LORD your God' supplies the Deuteronomic counterpart to imitating God as beloved children. Faint verbal contact; flagged because the prompt invokes the broader Deuteronomic perfection-before-God strand undergirding the imitatio Dei command.

echoes.text: You shall burn the whole ram on the altar: it is a burnt offering to Yahweh; it is a pleasant aroma, an offering made by fire to Yahweh.
echoes.note: Christ's self-offering as 'a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling fragrance' directly takes up the cultic formula for the ram of ordination, 'a burnt offering... a pleasing aroma, an offering by fire to the LORD.' High volume (the technical sacrificial idiom osme euodias) and recurrence across the Pentateuch make this a clear cultic appropriation applied to Christ.

echoes.text: Yahweh smelled the pleasant aroma. Yahweh said in his heart, “I will not again curse the ground any more for man’s sake because the imagination of man’s heart is evil from his youth; neither will I ever again strike every living thing, as I have done.
echoes.note: The LORD smelling the 'pleasing aroma' of Noah's sacrifice is the originating instance of the soothing-odor motif that the offering language evokes. Moderate volume; the phrase is the same Septuagintal idiom, reinforcing the sacrificial frame even if Exodus/Leviticus are the nearer source.

echoes.text: As a pleasant aroma will I accept you, when I bring you out from the peoples, and gather you out of the countries in which you have been scattered; and I will be sanctified in you in the sight of the nations.
echoes.note: 'As a pleasing aroma I will accept you' transfers the fragrant-offering language from animal sacrifice to God's acceptance of his people, a move parallel to Christ's self-gift accepted by God. Coherence is strong with Ephesians' ecclesial reading; medium confidence given multiple Levitical loci.

echoes.text: Yet it pleased Yahweh to bruise him. He has caused him to suffer. When you make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed. He shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of Yahweh shall prosper in his hand.
echoes.note: The Servant who makes himself 'an offering for sin' and 'gave himself up' undergirds the self-surrender Christology of 'gave himself up for us.' Coherence with the sacrificial/atonement frame is high; medium because the verbal tie runs through the wider Servant tradition rather than a single lemma.

echoes.text: Sacrifice and offering you didn’t desire. You have opened my ears. You have not required burnt offering and sin offering.
echoes.note: The contrast of obedient self-offering over against cultic sacrifice ('sacrifice and offering you did not desire') faintly colors Christ's acceptable self-gift. Low volume and contested, since Ephesians affirms rather than relativizes sacrifice; included for the offering/will-of-God nexus.
echoes.lxxText: Sacrifice and offering thou wouldest not; but a body hast thou prepared me: whole-burnt-offering and sacrifice for sin thou didst not require.

pericopes.text: But sexual immorality, and all uncleanness, or covetousness, let it not even be mentioned among you, as becomes saints; nor filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not appropriate; but rather giving of thanks. Know this for sure, that no sexually immoral person, nor unclean person, nor covetous man, who is an idolater, has any inheritance in the Kingdom of Christ and God. Let no one deceive you with empty words. For because of these things, the wrath of God comes on the children of disobedience. Therefore don’t be partakers with them.

echoes.text: Israel stayed in Shittim; and the people began to play the prostitute with the daughters of Moab;
echoes.note: The pairing of sexual immorality with idolatry (porneia leading to idol-worship at Baal-Peor) is the paradigmatic OT linkage that Ephesians compresses in 'covetousness, who is an idolater.' Faint and conceptual; flagged for the immorality-idolatry coherence rather than verbal contact.

echoes.text: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife. Neither shall you desire your neighbor’s house, his field, or his male servant, or his female servant, his ox, or his donkey, or anything that is your neighbor’s.”
echoes.note: 'You shall not covet' stands behind the catalogue's singling out of pleonexia, which Ephesians equates with idolatry. Coherence is strong with the Decalogue's covetousness/idolatry juxtaposition; medium volume given the term's broad Hellenistic-Jewish moral usage.

echoes.text: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that is your neighbor’s.”
echoes.note: The tenth commandment against coveting grounds the identification of greed as idolatry. Parallel to Deuteronomy 5:21; recurrence of the covet/idol pairing across the Decalogue tradition supports the link.

echoes.text: For it is a rebellious people, lying children, children who will not hear Yahweh’s law;
echoes.note: 'Rebellious people... children who will not hear the instruction of the LORD' supplies the Septuagintal background for 'children of disobedience' on whom wrath comes. Low volume; the idiom is a Semitic 'sons of' construction the prompt highlights for the wrath-on-disobedience strand.

pericopes.text: For you were once darkness, but are now light in the Lord. Walk as children of light, for the fruit of the Spirit is in all goodness and righteousness and truth, proving what is well pleasing to the Lord. Have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather even reprove them. For the things which are done by them in secret, it is a shame even to speak of. But all things, when they are reproved, are revealed by the light, for everything that reveals is light. Therefore he says, “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.”

echoes.text: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. Those who lived in the land of the shadow of death, on them the light has shined.
echoes.note: 'You were once darkness, but are now light' draws on 'the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light,' the prophetic light/darkness reversal. High coherence with Ephesians' conversion-as-illumination motif and strong verbal volume in the light/walk pairing.

echoes.text: “Arise, shine; for your light has come, and Yahweh’s glory is risen on you.
echoes.note: 'Arise, shine, for your light has come' anchors both the light-children theme here and explicitly the hymn of v.14. The Septuagintal phoatizou/anastethi cluster is verbally present; high volume and recurrence make Isaiah 60 a primary source for the section.

echoes.text: For, behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the peoples; but Yahweh will arise on you, and his glory shall be seen on you.
echoes.note: 'Darkness shall cover the earth... but the LORD will arise upon you' continues the darkness-over-against-light contrast that structures 5:8-11. Medium volume; reinforces the Isaian source of the whole light/darkness paraenesis.

echoes.text: Woe to those who deeply hide their counsel from Yahweh, and whose works are in the dark, and who say, “Who sees us?” and “Who knows us?”
echoes.note: 'Woe to those who hide deep their counsel from the LORD, whose deeds are in the dark' lies behind 'the unfruitful works of darkness... done in secret.' Coherence is strong (hidden/secret deeds exposed by light); medium confidence given thematic rather than lexical tie.

echoes.text: “These are of those who rebel against the light. They don’t know its ways, nor stay in its paths. The murderer rises with the light. He kills the poor and needy. In the night he is like a thief. The eye also of the adulterer waits for the twilight, saying, ‘No eye shall see me.’ He disguises his face. In the dark they dig through houses. They shut themselves up in the daytime. They don’t know the light. For the morning is to all of them like thick […]
echoes.note: Job's 'rebels against the light' who work murder and adultery in darkness, for whom morning is deep darkness, supplies the wisdom topos of secret works of darkness exposed. Medium volume; coherent with Ephesians' light-reveals-shameful-deeds logic.

echoes.text: Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.
echoes.note: 'Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead' (v.14) takes up 'Your dead shall live... awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust,' the resurrection-awakening oracle. High coherence with the rouse-from-death imagery; a leading source for the cited hymn.

echoes.text: Awake, awake, stand up, Jerusalem, that have drunk at the hand of Yahweh the cup of his wrath; you have drunken the bowl of the cup of staggering, and drained it.
echoes.note: 'Rouse yourself, rouse yourself, stand up, O Jerusalem' contributes the awakening-summons cadence behind 'Awake, you who sleep.' Medium volume; one of the clustered Isaian wake-up calls underlying the v.14 hymn.

echoes.text: Awake, awake, put on your strength, Zion; put on your beautiful garments, Jerusalem, the holy city: for henceforth there shall no more come into you the uncircumcised and the unclean.
echoes.note: 'Awake, awake, put on your strength, O Zion' is the paired imperatival summons (egeirou) that, with 60:1, shapes the hymnic 'Awake... and Christ will shine on you.' Coherence with the awakening-then-glory sequence is strong.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: 'Many who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake' offers an apocalyptic resurrection idiom for the sleeper rising from the dead in v.14. Low volume relative to the Isaian sources; flagged for the sleep-then-awake-from-death recurrence.

echoes.text: But to you who fear my name shall the sun of righteousness arise with healing in its wings. You will go out, and leap like calves of the stall.
echoes.note: 'The sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings' faintly informs 'Christ will shine on you' (epiphausei). Low volume and contested; included for the rising-light-upon-the-awakened motif.

echoes.text: But the path of the righteous is like the dawning light, that shines more and more until the perfect day.
echoes.note: 'The path of the righteous is like the light of dawn, shining brighter' supports the 'walk as children of light' / 'fruit of light in goodness and righteousness' wisdom imagery. Low confidence; thematic coherence with the righteous-walk-in-light topos.

pericopes.text: Therefore watch carefully how you walk, not as unwise, but as wise; redeeming the time, because the days are evil. Therefore don’t be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is.

echoes.text: The king answered, I know of a certainty that you would gain time, because you see the thing is gone from me.
echoes.note: 'You are trying to gain time' (kairon hymeis exagorazete) supplies the rare Septuagintal idiom behind 'redeeming the time' (ton kairon exagorazomenoi). Low volume but a genuine lexical parallel the prompt flags; contested because the sense is repurposed positively.

echoes.text: Therefore a prudent person keeps silent in such a time, for it is an evil time.
echoes.note: 'The prudent will keep silent in such a time, for it is an evil time' parallels 'redeeming the time, because the days are evil.' Coherence in the wise-conduct-in-an-evil-time motif; low volume and contested.

echoes.text: that the wise man may hear, and increase in learning; that the man of understanding may attain to sound counsel:
echoes.note: The wise/unwise contrast and the call to 'understand' echo wisdom's exhortation to gain prudence. Faint; included for the walk-wisely paraenesis drawing on the wisdom tradition.

pericopes.text: Don’t be drunken with wine, in which is dissipation, but be filled with the Spirit, speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs; singing, and making melody in your heart to the Lord; giving thanks always concerning all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to God, even the Father; subjecting yourselves one to another in the fear of Christ.

echoes.text: Don’t look at the wine when it is red, when it sparkles in the cup, when it goes down smoothly.
echoes.note: 'Do not look at wine when it is red... in the end it bites like a serpent' grounds the prohibition 'Do not be drunk with wine, in which is dissipation (asotia).' Coherence with the wisdom warning against drunkenness is strong; medium volume.

echoes.text: They also reel with wine, and stagger with strong drink. The priest and the prophet reel with strong drink. They are swallowed up by wine. They stagger with strong drink. They err in vision. They stumble in judgment.
echoes.note: 'They reel with wine and stagger with strong drink... they err in vision' supplies the prophetic picture of drunkenness as spiritual derangement, contrasted here with being filled with the Spirit. Medium coherence; the wine-versus-prophetic-Spirit antithesis is apt.

echoes.text: Wine is a mocker, and beer is a brawler. Whoever is led astray by them is not wise.
echoes.note: 'Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler' reinforces the wisdom condemnation of drunkenness behind the prohibition. Low volume; a recurrent sapiential warning rather than a specific quotation.

echoes.text: Sing to him a new song. Play skillfully with a shout of joy!
echoes.note: 'Sing to him a new song, play skillfully' stands behind 'psalms and hymns and spiritual songs... making melody in your heart.' The psalmos/odes vocabulary and the heart-singing motif show coherence with the psalter's worship language; medium volume.

echoes.text: Sing to Yahweh a new song! Sing to Yahweh, all the earth.
echoes.note: 'Sing to the LORD a new song' is the recurrent psalter summons that the trio of psalms/hymns/songs evokes. Low volume given many parallel psalm-headings (psalmos, hymnos, ode) in the Septuagint; flagged for recurrence.

echoes.text: I will bless Yahweh at all times. His praise will always be in my mouth.
echoes.note: 'I will bless the LORD at all times; his praise shall continually be in my mouth' parallels 'giving thanks always concerning all things.' Faint thematic coherence with continual thanksgiving; low confidence.

pericopes.text: Wives, be subject to your own husbands, as to the Lord. For the husband is the head of the wife, and Christ also is the head of the assembly, being himself the savior of the body. But as the assembly is subject to Christ, so let the wives also be to their own husbands in everything.

echoes.text: To the woman he said, “I will greatly multiply your pain in childbirth. In pain you will bear children. Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you.”
echoes.note: 'Your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you' offers the OT backdrop for the wifely-subjection and husband-as-head household instruction. Low volume and conceptual; contested because Ephesians grounds order in Christ rather than the curse.

pericopes.text: Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the assembly, and gave himself up for it; that he might sanctify it, having cleansed it by the washing of water with the word, that he might present the assembly to himself gloriously, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without defect. Even so husbands also ought to love their own wives as their own bodies. He who loves his own wife loves himself. For no man ever hated his own flesh; but nourishes and cherishes it, even as the Lord also does the assembly; because we are members of his body, of his flesh and bones.

echoes.text: Then washed I you with water; yes, I thoroughly washed away your blood from you, and I anointed you with oil.
echoes.note: 'I bathed you with water and washed off your blood' is the bridal-bath image behind Christ cleansing the church 'by the washing of water with the word' to present her gloriously. Coherence with the Lord-as-bridegroom adorning his bride is strong; medium volume.

echoes.text: Now when I passed by you, and looked at you, behold, your time was the time of love; and I spread my skirt over you, and covered your nakedness: yes, I swore to you, and entered into a covenant with you, says the Lord Yahweh, and you became mine.
echoes.note: 'I spread my garment over you... and entered into a covenant with you, and you became mine' supplies the covenant-marriage frame for Christ's love of the church as bride. Coherent with the present-her-to-himself motif; medium confidence.

echoes.text: You are all beautiful, my love. There is no spot in you.
echoes.note: 'You are altogether beautiful, my love; there is no flaw in you' lies behind presenting the church 'not having spot or wrinkle... holy and without defect.' Coherence with the flawless-bride imagery is high; medium volume since the diction is reworked.

echoes.text: Whoever offers a sacrifice of peace offerings to Yahweh to accomplish a vow, or for a freewill offering, of the herd or of the flock, it shall be perfect to be accepted. It shall have no defect.
echoes.note: The sacrificial requirement that an offering be 'without blemish' colors the church presented 'without spot... and without defect' (amomos). Low volume; flagged for the cultic blamelessness vocabulary applied to the bride.

echoes.text: I will betroth you to me forever. Yes, I will betroth you to me in righteousness, in justice, in loving kindness, and in compassion.
echoes.note: 'I will betroth you to me forever... in righteousness' contributes to the divine-marriage typology underlying Christ and the church. Low volume; one of the prophetic bridegroom-of-Israel texts cohering with the passage.

pericopes.text: “For this cause a man will leave his father and mother, and will be joined to his wife. The two will become one flesh.” This mystery is great, but I speak concerning Christ and of the assembly. Nevertheless each of you must also love his own wife even as himself; and let the wife see that she respects her husband.

echoes.text: Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh.
echoes.note: 'For this cause a man will leave his father and mother, and will be joined to his wife, and the two will become one flesh' is a verbatim Septuagintal citation introduced as scripture. Maximal volume and explicit quotation; the cornerstone OT text for the one-flesh/Christ-and-church mystery.

pericopes.text: Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. “Honor your father and mother,” which is the first commandment with a promise: “that it may be well with you, and you may live long on the earth.” You fathers, don’t provoke your children to wrath, but nurture them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.

echoes.text: “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which Yahweh your God gives you.
echoes.note: Verses 2-3 quote the Decalogue commandment verbatim from the LXX: 'Honor your father and mother, that it may be well with you and that you may live long.' Volume is maximal (explicit citation formula 'which is the first commandment with a promise'). Paul reads the Sinai command as still binding catechesis for Christian households.

echoes.text: “Honor your father and your mother, as Yahweh your God commanded you; that your days may be long, and that it may go well with you, in the land which Yahweh your God gives you.
echoes.note: The Deuteronomic recension of the Fifth Commandment is the more exact verbal parallel: it adds 'that it may be well with you' (eu soi genetai), which Eph 6:3 reproduces against Exodus' shorter form. The dual availability of both Decalogue versions explains Paul's conflated wording; Deuteronomy supplies the well-being clause.

echoes.text: and you shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.
echoes.note: The charge to fathers to 'nurture them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord' (6:4) coheres with the Shema's command to teach the commandments diligently to one's children. The thematic link (paternal catechesis) is strong but verbal contact is faint, so an echo rather than allusion.

echoes.text: My son, don’t despise Yahweh’s discipline, neither be weary of his reproof: for whom Yahweh loves, he reproves; even as a father reproves the son in whom he delights.
echoes.note: Fatherly 'discipline and instruction of the Lord' (paideia... kyriou, 6:4) echoes the wisdom tradition's language of the Lord's paideia of a son. Recurrence of paideia across Proverbs LXX supports coherence, though no single verse is quoted.
echoes.lxxText: My son, despise not the chastening of the Lord; nor faint when thou art rebuked of him: for whom the Lord loves, he rebukes, and scourges every son whom he receives.

echoes.text: One who spares the rod hates his son, but one who loves him is careful to discipline him.
echoes.note: The instruction not to 'provoke children to wrath' but to nurture them tempers the wisdom theme of disciplined child-rearing found in Proverbs. The connection is conceptual coherence within the household-instruction tradition, hence a faint, contested echo.

echoes.text: Hear me your father, O my children, And do thereafter, that you may be saved. For the Lord has given the father glory as touching the children, And has confirmed the judgement of the mother as touching the sons. He that honors his father will make atonement for sins: And he that gives glory to his mother is as one that lays up treasure. Whoso honors his father will have joy of his children; And in the day of his prayer he will be heard. He that gives […]
echoes.note: Sirach's extended meditation on honoring father and mother, with its promise of long life and atonement, stands in the Second-Temple stream that mediated the Decalogue command into household ethics. Availability (deuterocanon) and thematic coherence are real, but Paul cites the Decalogue directly, so Sirach is background not source.

pericopes.text: Servants, be obedient to those who according to the flesh are your masters, with fear and trembling, in singleness of your heart, as to Christ; not in the way of service only when eyes are on you, as men pleasers; but as servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart; with good will doing service, as to the Lord, and not to men; knowing that whatever good thing each one does, he will receive the same again from the Lord, whether he is bound or free. You masters, do the same things to them, and give up threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and there is no partiality with him.

echoes.text: For Yahweh your God, he is God of gods, and Lord of lords, the great God, the mighty, and the awesome, who doesn’t respect persons, nor takes reward.
echoes.note: The assurance that the heavenly Master shows 'no partiality' (prosopolempsia, 6:9) draws on the LXX formula 'God... does not show partiality' (ou thaumazei prosopon). Volume is high via the distinctive divine-impartiality idiom; Paul applies the courtroom maxim to dissolve master/slave status before God.

echoes.text: Now therefore let the fear of Yahweh be on you. Take heed and do it: for there is no iniquity with Yahweh our God, nor respect of persons, nor taking of bribes.”
echoes.note: Jehoshaphat's charge to judges grounds impartial justice in the fact that 'with the LORD our God there is no... partiality' (ouk estin... lempsis prosopou). The same theologoumenon underlies 6:9; recurrence of the formula across the OT strengthens coherence, though Deuteronomy is the primary verbal source.

echoes.text: You shall not rule over him with harshness, but shall fear your God.
echoes.note: Masters told to 'give up threatening' (6:9) coheres with the Holiness Code's prohibition on ruling over a fellow Israelite 'with harshness/rigor,' grounded likewise in fear of God. The ethical shape matches but no verbal quotation occurs, so a faint echo.

echoes.text: “If I have despised the cause of my male servant or of my female servant, when they contended with me; What then shall I do when God rises up? When he visits, what shall I answer him? Didn’t he who made me in the womb make him? Didn’t one fashion us in the womb?
echoes.note: Job's refusal to despise the case of his servant, because the same God made both master and slave in the womb, anticipates Eph 6:9's leveling of master and slave before their common heavenly Master. Coherence is strong; verbal dependence is absent, so a contested echo.

pericopes.text: Finally, be strong in the Lord, and in the strength of his might. Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil. For our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities, against the powers, against the world’s rulers of the darkness of this age, and against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. Therefore put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day, and, having done all, to stand.

echoes.text: “Be strong and courageous; for you shall cause this people to inherit the land which I swore to their fathers to give them. Only be strong and very courageous, to observe to do according to all the law, which Moses my servant commanded you. Don’t turn from it to the right hand or to the left, that you may have good success wherever you go. This book of the law shall not depart out of your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may […]
echoes.note: The opening exhortation 'be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might' (6:10) echoes the repeated divine charge to Joshua 'be strong and courageous' (ischye kai andrizou) as he takes the land. The martial 'stand firm' framing of the whole passage coheres with the conquest setting, though the wording is a stock LXX encouragement formula.

echoes.text: But those who wait for Yahweh will renew their strength. They will mount up with wings like eagles. They will run, and not be weary. They will walk, and not faint.
echoes.note: 'In the strength of his might' (en to kratei tes ischyos autou, 6:10) resonates with Isaiah's promise that those who wait on the Lord 'shall renew their strength.' The verbal contact is thematic (divine strengthening of the weak) rather than lexical, so a faint echo.

echoes.text: But the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me twenty-one days; but, behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me: and I remained there with the kings of Persia.
echoes.note: The cosmic conflict 'not against flesh and blood but against the principalities... rulers of the darkness' (6:12) coheres with Daniel's angelic 'princes' (archontes) of Persia and Greece who war in the heavens. Second-Temple angelology of national powers supplies availability; the connection is conceptual, hence a contested echo.

echoes.text: He put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head; and he put on garments of vengeance for clothing, and was clad with zeal as a mantle.
echoes.note: The command to 'put on the whole armor of God' (endysasthe... panoplian tou theou, 6:11,13) draws its core image from Isaiah's Divine Warrior who 'put on righteousness as a breastplate and a helmet of salvation,' and from Wisdom's elaboration of God arming creation. The arming verb endysasthai and the panoply frame derive from this Divine-Warrior tradition before the individual pieces are named.

echoes.text: He will take his jealousy as complete armor, And will make the whole creation his weapons for vengeance on his enemies: He will put on righteousness as a breastplate, And will array himself with judgement unfeigned as with a helmet; He will take holiness as an invincible shield, And he will sharpen stern wrath for a sword: And the world will go forth with him to fight against his insensate foes.
echoes.note: Wisdom expands Isaiah 59:17 into a full panoply: the Lord 'will take his zeal as a panoply (panoplian) and arm creation,' donning righteousness as breastplate and impartial judgment as helmet. Paul's distinctive word panoplia and the assembled set of pieces show direct dependence on this Second-Temple development, not Isaiah alone.

pericopes.text: Stand therefore, having the utility belt of truth buckled around your waist, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, and having fitted your feet with the preparation of the Good News of peace; above all, taking up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to quench all the fiery darts of the evil one. And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God;

echoes.text: Righteousness will be the belt of his waist, and faithfulness the belt of his waist.
echoes.note: 'The belt of truth buckled around your waist' (6:14) draws on the messianic shoot of Jesse who wears 'righteousness as the belt of his waist and faithfulness/truth the belt of his loins.' Volume is high: the girdle imagery and the pairing with truth/righteousness are distinctive to Isaiah 11, and Paul redistributes its terms across belt and breastplate.

echoes.text: He put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head; and he put on garments of vengeance for clothing, and was clad with zeal as a mantle.
echoes.note: 'The breastplate of righteousness' (6:14) is a direct lift of the Divine Warrior who 'put on righteousness as a breastplate' (enedysato dikaiosynen hos thoraka). The lexical match (thorax dikaiosynes) is exact, making this a high-volume allusion; the believer is clothed in God's own armor.

echoes.text: He will put on righteousness as a breastplate, And will array himself with judgement unfeigned as with a helmet;
echoes.note: Wisdom's reworking of Isaiah ('he will put on righteousness as a breastplate') is the proximate Second-Temple form Paul knows, reinforcing the breastplate piece. Recurrence of the Isaiah image through Wisdom strengthens coherence even where Isaiah is the ultimate source.

echoes.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”
echoes.note: 'Feet fitted with the readiness of the gospel of peace' (6:15) alludes to Isaiah's herald, 'how beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news... who proclaims peace.' The triad feet + euangelizomenos + peace is distinctive to this verse; the 'shoes' piece evangelizes the warrior's stance.

echoes.text: Behold, on the mountains the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace! Keep your feasts, Judah! Perform your vows, for the wicked one will no more pass through you. He is utterly cut off.
echoes.note: Nahum 2:1 LXX (1:15 EVV) repeats Isaiah's herald motif: 'behold upon the mountains the feet of one bringing good news and announcing peace.' Its near-identical wording strengthens the 'gospel of peace' shoe imagery, though Isaiah 52:7 is the primary source.

echoes.text: He has also prepared for himself the instruments of death. He makes ready his flaming arrows.
echoes.note: The 'shield of faith' that quenches 'all the flaming darts of the evil one' (6:16) coheres with the Psalmist's image of God making his arrows into 'flaming/fiery shafts.' The unusual 'flaming darts' (belos pepyromena) motif has its nearest OT background here, though the attacker is reversed; a faint echo.

echoes.text: After these things Yahweh’s word came to Abram in a vision, saying, “Don’t be afraid, Abram. I am your shield, your exceedingly great reward.”
echoes.note: The 'shield of faith' (thyreos tes pisteos, 6:16) may evoke the LORD's word to Abram, 'I am your shield,' the foundational pairing of shield and faith (Abram 'believed'). Coherence with the faith motif is suggestive but the lexical contact is generic, so a low-confidence echo.

echoes.text: He put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head; and he put on garments of vengeance for clothing, and was clad with zeal as a mantle.
echoes.note: 'Take the helmet of salvation' (perikephalaian tou soteriou, 6:17) is a verbatim borrowing from the Divine Warrior who set 'a helmet of salvation on his head' (perikephalaian soteriou). The exact lexical match makes this among the clearest pieces of Isaianic armor; God's saving victory becomes the believer's headgear.

echoes.text: He will put on righteousness as a breastplate, And will array himself with judgement unfeigned as with a helmet;
echoes.note: Wisdom 5:18 also gives the warrior 'impartial judgment as a helmet,' confirming the Second-Temple currency of the helmet image alongside Isaiah. Recurrence supports coherence though Isaiah supplies the exact 'helmet of salvation.'

echoes.text: and he has made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand, he has hidden me: and he has made me a polished shaft; in his quiver has he kept me close:
echoes.note: 'The sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God' (6:17) draws on the Servant who says God 'made my mouth like a sharp sword.' The fusion of sword + the spoken word of God is distinctive to this Servant Song; the believer wields the prophetic word as weapon.

echoes.text: but with righteousness he will judge the poor, and decide with equity for the humble of the earth. He will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth; and with the breath of his lips he will kill the wicked.
echoes.note: The messianic shoot strikes the earth 'with the rod of his mouth' and slays the wicked 'with the breath (pneumati) of his lips,' joining sword/word with Spirit (pneuma) precisely as Eph 6:17 ('sword of the Spirit... word of God'). The Spirit-word-judgment cluster strengthens the allusion alongside Isaiah 49:2.

echoes.text: Therefore I have cut them to pieces with the prophets; I killed them with the words of my mouth. Your judgments are like a flash of lightning.
echoes.note: God's killing/hewing of the people 'by the words of my mouth' provides a further prophetic precedent for the word of God as a slaying weapon, supporting the sword image. The contact is thematic recurrence rather than verbal dependence, hence a faint echo.

pericopes.text: with all prayer and requests, praying at all times in the Spirit, and being watchful to this end in all perseverance and requests for all the saints: on my behalf, that utterance may be given to me in opening my mouth, to make known with boldness the mystery of the Good News, for which I am an ambassador in chains; that in it I may speak boldly, as I ought to speak.

echoes.text: When Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house (now his windows were open in his room toward Jerusalem) and he kneeled on his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did before.
echoes.note: 'Praying at all times in the Spirit... in all perseverance' (6:18) coheres with the OT pattern of unceasing, regular prayer exemplified by Daniel's thrice-daily petition. The connection is to a devotional topos rather than a specific text, so a faint echo.

echoes.text: Let my prayer be set before you like incense; the lifting up of my hands like the evening sacrifice.
echoes.note: The summons to constant 'prayer and requests... at all times' (6:18) resonates with the Psalmist's plea that prayer rise continually like incense. Thematic coherence with perpetual supplication supports a low-confidence, contested echo.

echoes.text: But when I speak with you, I will open your mouth, and you shall tell them, Thus says the Lord Yahweh: He who hears, let him hear; and he who forbears, let him forbear: for they are a rebellious house.
echoes.note: Paul's request that 'utterance may be given me in opening my mouth' to make known the mystery with boldness (6:19) echoes the prophetic call in which God opens the prophet's mouth to speak his word. The mouth-opening / divinely given speech motif coheres with prophetic commissioning, though no single verse is quoted.

pericopes.text: But that you also may know my affairs, how I am doing, Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful servant in the Lord, will make known to you all things; whom I have sent to you for this very purpose, that you may know our state, and that he may comfort your hearts. Peace be to the brothers, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace be with all those who love our Lord Jesus Christ with incorruptible love. Amen.

echoes.text: ‘Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’
echoes.note: The closing benediction 'Peace be to the brothers, and love with faith... Grace be with all' (6:23-24) stands in the stream of the Aaronic blessing's peace-and-grace formula. The contact is to a liturgical convention rather than a quotation, so a faint, contested echo.
